utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I understand that you have something to raise before the witness enters the courtroom. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you. Good morning to everyone. Before we start this working day, I would like to repeat once again because the transcript recorded the numbers of paragraphs and references to these documents wrong. We asked for 40 hours, reckoning that the report of this witness, including more than a thousand paragraphs and several thousand references and documents, is too important and practically blended with the indictment so that one cannot really distinguish between the report, the indictment, and the pre-trial brief. The witness confirmed himself that he was an investigator first and he cannot pin-point the moment when he was made an expert, and he was made an expert because it was too expensive to engage a different expert. The Defence cannot properly challenge this material unless we are given enough time. Each of these things can be disputed if we get enough time. We need at least an increase of time by one-third to prove why the report is wrong and what it should really look like. I'm afraid we would jeopardise the integrity of this process if we treat such important witnesses and such important material like this and if we are unable to challenge them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that nine hours is more than sufficient to cover all the important issues, and I think my understanding is that you have two and a half hours for today. And at the end of the session we'll see whether it would be necessary to give you the two sessions, but that's it for the moment. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I raise one quick matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution intends to respond to the 49th and 50th disclosure motions forthwith, but we have endeavoured to aggregate those and respond to the two motions together in light of that. We would orally at this point seek an extension for the word limit for that particular response that addresses both motions to approximately 5300 words. I have raised that matter with Mr. Robinson. The Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's granted, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, I'd like to let you know that we join in the motion for admission of documents from the bar table that the Prosecutor filed yesterday and we won't be filing anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the witness, may I remind everyone that we didn't admit D303. I would like to remind that on page 14393, beginning with line 21, this witness confirmed that both agreements from February and March were accepted by the Muslim side, by the SDA, and then reneged on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would just note, Mr. President, that that same document was raised, as I believe the Court noted, with Dr. Donia. The issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness can be brought in. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The issue of whether there was an agreement in principle, and then backing away is -- is not particularly at issue and was contained, I believe, in the witness's reports and testimony. So in light of the backdrop to this particular document that the Court noted and is aware of, if the accused is seeking to have that document admitted, it would appear that the Court's interest is in ensuring that the document has been addressed and that that brief reference to a matter that is broadly raised and has not been contested I understood did not seem sufficient for the Court, particularly in light of the issues raised in previous testimony about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that D303 is a "Politika" article. The reason why we did not admit it through Dr. Donia was that Dr. Donia was not able to give any confirmation as to the article itself or to the content thereof. But in this case the witness was able to comment upon that, and as such, we would admit it. And then that will be fully admitted. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina enacted on 28th of February was adopted based on the agreements already reached about the powers of the constituent units?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 28 [as interpreted] on page 62 of your document, 65 ter 592. You say: [In English] "Karadzic seemed to recognise this, telling the SDS Deputies Club on 28th of February, 'Please, until two or three months ago we were hoping to be able to play the Yugoslav card and to say the Yugoslav Army, Yugoslav legality,'" et cetera, "'this is slipping out of our grasp. This is why we started on another task, a Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, our sovereign right, our army. We are preparing the constitutional framework to be able to have immediately and on the basis of the negotiations in Lisbon, to have a national guard, to have our own police force, to have a government, to turn the Yugoslav Army into the Army of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina ...'" [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. It's paragraph 95. The record got it wrong and the page is 62. You quote in your report yourself what I said to the deputies, namely, that we cannot play the Yugoslav card anymore, that we should play the card of our sovereign rights in Bosnia, and that we would be working to prepare the constitution that would give us the right to a national government, a police force, an army based on the Lisbon Agreement? Do you remember the section in the Lisbon Agreement about the jurisdiction of different entities implies that we would have our own police force?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no agreement. It was denounced shortly after it was reached and it was -- so there was no final agreement and I don't think it was even framed as a final agreement. It was very similar to the later agreement which was simply bases for negotiation. The preparation and the establishment of separate Bosnian Serb institutions had been going on, as we've seen in the course of my testimony, for quite some months. And indeed, meetings were held -- or at least one meeting was held as early as October 1991 on establishing a separate -- a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Bosnia. So I don't see the adoption of this particular law as in any way executing or being based on the -- the Lisbon -- so-called Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you confirmed yesterday that the only thing left to negotiate on were maps, that maps should be specified. Do you remember that the Serbs were prepared to accept the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina although they had been deceived and that their basic condition was not met, that they should have their constituent unit? That's what Ajanovic himself thinks.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I said the only thing left to be negotiated were the maps. The Sarajevo Agreement paper that we saw included a great number of points, including the map, all of which were to serve as a basis for further negotiations. So I'm under the impression that even on the basis of that document, if it had been adhered to, negotiations could have continued in relation to all those points that we saw yesterday. The agreement was basically denounced rather quickly by both the Muslim and Croatian sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, the Croatian side never denounced the agreement. The agreement was called "Agreed Principles." There were no more negotiations about that. Only the map was to be negotiated.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I can only refer to the text of the document. It says right at the end of the document that it's to serve as a basis for further negotiations, and the negotiations did continue in Brussels on March the 30th or 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if my question was recorded fully on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see D269 in e-court, just in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, while we're waiting for the document, we saw how the constitutional crisis developed in Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, how Yugoslavia came into being, how Bosnia and Herzegovina came into being, and what its nature was as the republic of three different peoples. Now let's see the evolution of my state of mind that you had an insight into and you were able to include it in your report. Let's look at this document on the screen. [In English] "The Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed last week /or last Sunday/ in Sarajevo. Dr. Radovan Karadzic was elected its leader," and so on. "What are the programme and organisational and political characteristics of the SDS ..." [Interpretation] Would you please look at this. Just cast a glance at this to see how the state of mind of Radovan Karadzic evolved over this crisis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 68 -- sorry, page 8 in English. Page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The Serbs and Muslims are basically not in a conflict of interest. Regardless of what may happen, the Serbs and the Muslims will always live in a common state and they know how and they will know in future how to live together. There is no need for a third party to fix things between them." This was an interview given to the weekly "Nin." It was on the 20th of July, 1990, a week after the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party. I gave an interview to the weekly "Nin" of Belgrade, saying how I see the new era in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Treanor take into account this interview as one of the earliest interviews where I expressed my political views on the co-existence of Serbs and Muslims in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I've read this interview. I can't recall offhand whether it's cited in any of my reports, but the view that we see expressed here is reflective of what I believe I said in my testimony so far, that is, originally the wish of the Bosnian Serbs was for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain a republic in Yugoslavia. At this time, that is, in July 1990, preparations were being made for the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The main opponent at those elections was seen, I believe, by all the newly formed non-Communist party as being the Communist party. They were afraid that there would be very sorts of chicanery and fraud, perhaps, to try to steal the election for the Communists. And the non-Communist parties in this case or concretely the main parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, formed a coalition in order to help prevent that, to guarantee that the non-Communists would have a majority and they at this point in time were all being very nice to each other. There was no reason for them not to be nice to each other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Treanor, my question is: Did you note and record in your report the initial political views of Radovan Karadzic on the co-existence of the Serbs and Muslims and was the SDA at that moment also in favour of Yugoslavia? Did you put it in your report, the state of mind of Radovan Karadzic? This was a week after the establishment of the party. No challenges, no threats; other people threatened Yugoslavia, the Muslims and the SDA. How did my attitude to the crisis evolve? The basic question: Did you take this into account and did you put in your report the evolution of my state of mind? Did you record this initial view I held on co-existence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I think the basic position of the SDS at this time on -- wishing that Bosnia remain in -- as a whole in Yugoslavia is included in the report. As I said, I have -- I have read this interview and I at this point can't remember exactly what might be said about it in particular, but nevertheless, the fundamental point that the SDS wished that the whole of Bosnia remain in BH is reflected in the reports. And I've noted the -- the change that took place in their immediate goals after the plebiscite. The plebiscite confirmed that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, sir, please, I am indicted here, not the SDS. I am indicted for intolerance towards Croats and Muslims, and this is the declaration of Radovan Karadzic on Muslims and Croats that you did not put in your report. I'm saying that we have no disagreement with the Muslims and that we can live together with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 40129, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is not you that is giving evidence now. Put your questions. The last comment is improper, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'm in a hurry because I have no time and the witness is using up my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Dr. Treanor, are you aware that I am indicted -- I'm accused of being intolerant towards the Muslims? And here you have my view recorded on how I actually viewed co-existence with the Muslims. When did you -- where did you see that I was intolerant towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's the question asked and answered. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 40129. 65 ter 40129. Can it be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that I would like to ask you, in your testimony in the Brdjanin case on page 21034, lines 12 through 18 of the transcript: [In English] "We put in the report what we believed to be relevant, within the scope of trying to keep the report to a reasonable length. If we got involved in putting in a footnote or something, every document that we could possibly find on every issue, it would be a massive and unwieldy report and certain a massive and unwieldy documentary annex to the report. One of the duties is certainly to keep our eyes open for any exculpatory evidence." [Interpretation] Now I'm asking you, Dr. Treanor, did you meet that obligation? Did you note what I'm going to put to you now as I put concerning the previous document, my views on these issues, especially our co-existence with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, please. 4 in English and 3 in Serbian. 0:27:38 is the time. Radovan Karadzic says: "Ladies and gentlemen, distinguished Assembly, this plot to separate Yugoslavia had begun. With the new constitutions in Slovenia and Croatia ... the final blows are being inflicted on Yugoslavia which is expecting to" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic give the interpreters a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters are struggling to find the reference. I think it's time code 00:27:38.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Next page of the Serbian, please. "The former generals, the current statesmen of our republic, are threatening the Serbian people with civil war. The Serbian people should not be threatened with civil war. They will take that seriously. It is absolutely clear to us against whom General Tudjman would be waging the civil war ..." And then further down: "They changed the essence of the borders, the quality and nature of our internal borders. So the administrative lines which are supposed to join us have been transformed or will soon be transformed into firm state borders which separate us. The gentlemen are interested in the shape of the border and whether the border is on this or the other side of the stream or field rather than in preserving the nature of those borders which are internal, administrative lines between brotherly peoples ..." Now, in that speech delivered at that Assembly, did you take note and record that position of mine? Or did you decide on your own that this is not exculpatory material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I think this document may be referenced in the reports, but it certainly reflects the view that I have put forward in the reports, that the SDS wished to keep the whole of Bosnia within Yugoslavia. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence considers --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I believe that the -- one thing I can recall specifically on this is the speech of Mr. Milosevic in which he refers to this issue of administrative borders not being suitable for being international borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, it is my state of mind here and my conduct and behaviour. So your report - and it's hundreds of paragraphs - refers to me. And it was your duty, you were duty-bound, to record everything that went to my advantage which you did not do. Let me ask you: Did you have access to this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 65 ter 938 next, please. Page 2 of the English, please, and of the Serbian. It has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, it says: "The position of the Serbs in Yugoslavia." It's a public rally of the Serbian Democratic Party held in the middle of Sarajevo. Mrs. Plavsic, Koljevic, and so on were present, held a lecture on the position of the Serbs in BH. And then it says: "It is -- tragic is the fate of a country which demands the rejecting of any people let alone the biggest one as in the case of Yugoslavia. When they asked me as a psychologist if the Serbs fear that all the other people are against them is irrational, I maintain that it is not." And then I go on to say: "The Serbs cannot allow the Muslims to be proclaimed a majority people on the basis of the Ustasha genocide against the Serbs in World War II before which the Serbs were the majority people in Bosnia. We are a state-building people even if we are just 5, let alone 31 per cent" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see the bottom of that English page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now on civil war, I say: "I consider there will not be a civil war."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page for the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "My opinion is that it won't happen because the Serbs won't start the skirmish first and the others are afraid to. No one has reason to fear the Serbs if they have no misdeeds against them." Did you note this and record it in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 65 ter 30027, please. 30027.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this next document. It's a talk between President Milosevic and me, a conversation held on the 29th of May, 1991, and the long paragraph at the bottom, if we could focus on that. I'm informing President Milosevic there that Izetbegovic suddenly came out with a surprising proposal loud and clear, never louder and clearer than he did then, and he proposed that we divide up Bosnia and that we were astounded to hear that. Then we discussed what we should do. They said that we don't want to leave the -- we said we don't want to leave the federal Yugoslavia. They don't want to stay in federal Yugoslavia, and then today we continued the talks, and so on and so forth. Now, did you take note of this conversation where I am saying that Izetbegovic came out with a proposal to divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this conversation is cited in the report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to the next page, please, both in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: President Milosevic asks whether he wants to unite with Croatia towards the end there, and in English -- and then on next page. "I don't think he wants to unite with Croatia. He wants to use Croatia to leave Yugoslavia because he wanted -- he wants an enclave."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "He'd like to see -- to have one as a Muslim enclave in the valley of the river Bosna, which I think he needs for the Arab world."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He says: Yes, yes." And then Karadzic goes on to say: "Of course it would be a difficult negotiation and a great problem, how to use each principle. We didn't want to leave and we still believe that it would be a pity if Bosnia were to be divided. That is our basic stand, and when it comes to it, we will announce that everybody, every party, should announce their own position." Did you know this position of ours, that we thought it was a pity to divide Bosnia? And this is the end of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I said that I don't believe this particular conversation is referenced in the report. What seems to be under discussion here is the Bosnian Serb desire for the whole of Bosnia to remain within Yugoslavia. On the other hand, Izetbegovic does seem to be, as I think we've discussed here, pushing for independence from Yugoslavia and perhaps offering as a sweetener for such a deal on the part of the Bosnian Serbs to have some sort of regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now go down a bit on that page where Radovan Karadzic says: "All right, but now the situation is -- well, I think he is very cunning. He doesn't say what he -- those ultimate moves. Those last moves of his, the last intentions of an Islamic Republic. And he is hiding behind the state and citizens and there he is walking hand in hand with the communists." Next page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Karadzic says: "Well, I'm afraid, you see, you saw what happened with the army and with Tudjman, right? I'm afraid they're going to announce a unification and ask for assistance from Tudjman." Did you include the Islamic Declaration in your report and the state of mind of the Muslim leadership with respect to the administration of the country?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration, I don't think that's in the report, no. The interesting thing that is reflected here is the view of Dr. Karadzic of Mr. Izetbegovic as being an unreliable negotiating partner. Indeed, Mr. Izetbegovic seemed to make sudden reversals on any number of occasions, some of which we have discussed here, including the rejection of the Sarajevo -- the Lisbon and the Sarajevo Agreements during the Cutileiro negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Karadzic says: "And then to accuse the Serbs of keeping them as hostages in Yugoslavia," and they're referring to this possible alliance between Tudjman and Izetbegovic. "To accuse the Serbs of keeping them as hostages in Yugoslavia or that they're keeping them as -- or that they want to break up Bosnia in any way for whatever. Their biggest concern is to accuse us and we're not giving them any reason for that." And then somewhat lower down Karadzic goes on to say that: "Recognition for the top-most organs of power, that will be a nice thing. And I don't know what's happening with the army. Are they aware of how well armed they are?" And then further down: "This morning we caught a truck with arms and the policemen sort of clouded the issue. I cannot trace it anywhere." And then further down: "The Muslims are arming themselves." Doctor, did you know that Izetbegovic and Tudjman in June 1991 concluded a secret agreement and included President Kucan into that, a secret alliance against Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 1991, I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the Muslim officials considered that Bosnia should enter into war the moment that Croatia entered into war and that they made statements to that effect and that we have those statements?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I thought the position of the SDA at least was to remain neutral in the war, that is, the war going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we look at D270 for a brief moment. It's already been admitted but just to refresh our memories. D270.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between myself and Vitomir Zepinic, the Serbian deputy of the joint foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The minister of internal affairs, not foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope I said "internal affairs." He was the deputy of the minister of internal affairs on behalf of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English 10, Serbian 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I say: "I have to tell you this. Tomorrow I won't be able to be able to keep the Assembly together. In particular, I won't be able to keep the Serbian deputies together if things happen, things happen which the Serbian party in power, the ruling party ... it's the ruling party, it's not an outsider but a party that holds 35.65 per cent of the power."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says: "They are preparing for war. They have prepared a staff, and you don't know about that, you don't know where their staff is."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "They organised parallel television. Alija as already given TV statements from his war studio for the Yugoslav network. We know all about that. There is a huge number of armed people, there are preparations for war, preparations for war, there are drills to block barracks, there are counter-manoeuvres being carried out by the army, Armija, and here they are going to war and the Serbs will no longer ... tomorrow after the Assembly will resolve the issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... they want the unlawful way although we've proved to them that they cannot legally or politically carry that out. We have told them to use the constitutional procedure to change the constitution, but they have no chance."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "They have no chance with the international public or with the legal system. All they can do is trick us, but the Serbs will not allow them to do that tomorrow. And one of the fires I had to put out these days was the MUP issue, and tomorrow the deputies will certainly open up the issue of MUP." Now, did you have access to this intercepted conversation and did you take it on board and include it in your report, our knowledge that in June everything was, in fact, prepared for war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when this intercept was acquired, but in principle I had access to everything. I certainly did not cite these passages in the report. It's possible that the conversation itself may have been cited. I think there's some discussion in the report, in the original report, of some of the difficulties with MUP and Bosnian Serb dissatisfaction with what was going on there, especially with personnel issues. That's all I can say on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at the next page for a brief moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here it says: "Tomorrow is the question of the fate of BH, of Bosnia," Karadzic speaking. "I have no chance or way to change anything. Neither the people nor the deputies would accept any exception. Bosnia will remain in Yugoslavia until some of its peoples decide differently. And this will be seen clearly tomorrow. Tomorrow maybe the political system ... BH might collapse and then it will be chaos, but we can't do anything to help. We can't bow our heads. No chance of us doing that. We had no chance to change anything, nor do we have the right to do so. And if something is done which the people will not accept, there will be chaos in Bosnia." Now, this has already been admitted, but I just wanted to remind you of what the situation was like. And I'm talking to the deputy police minister who ought to know what was going on in the country. And you have not included this portion in your report either, have you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look at D271, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between me and Dr. Vukic, the regional head of the SDS for Krajina. And throughout this conversation I'm criticising them for helping Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 of the English and page 3 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Third line from the top, page 2 in English. I say: "I think that it's clear now that Izetbegovic wants war. " And a little further down I'm criticising the late Babic and saying: "Well, he is playing into the hands of this warmongering Izetbegovic." Now, do you know that I had to fight a battle with my peripheral organs, party organs, to have them act in conformity with the law so as not to give Izetbegovic a pretext for his warmongering?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the movement in Bosnian Krajina to unite with the Croatian Krajina, I was certainly aware of that and it was discussed in the report -- in the -- I believe in the leadership study. Perhaps there's something in the original report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to page 6 of the English and 7 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Karadzic says: "No, no. You can say that I talked to them and said that Alija was preparing for war and that he was seeking assistance for war ..." And I go on to say: "... because I'll accuse" -- after swearing I say: "... because I'll accuse them all of giving an incentive for Alija Izetbegovic to start the war." Now, this answer: "There are forces in Bosnia who know that they can't go ahead without war and they need a pretext for the war to put the blame on someone else. We must not give them this pretext." And then: "That's the basic thing, otherwise international law and our own constitutional law is on our side." Now, Dr. Treanor, am I advocating war here or am I advocating the avoidance of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what's going on here is citing arguments that were used with the people in Bosnian Krajina who wanted to go ahead and in order to -- with their unification with Croatian Krajina. To prevent them from doing that, these types of arguments were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were arguments used which were in favour of war or against war? Am I striving for peace and not creating causes for war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's basically what the argument is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have D273 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are stenographic notes from the Assembly of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 12th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to page 133 in English and 120 in Serbian. In e-court it's page 120 in Serbian, that's right, and it's the right page in English towards the top, the second paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "You see that this struggle is being fought in the parliament. It's good that it's being fought in the parliament rather than the streets. We will not do anything that would lead to the fight spilling over into the streets." Did you know about this speech? Did you note this position I took, that everything had to be kept within the parliament, that everything had to be done to prevent war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe this passage is cited in any of the reports. The document itself is, of course, referenced and used. I would just remind the Court that at this time, early July 1991, shortly after the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia, the outbreak of fighting in Slovenia and growing tension in Croatia, the JNA was attempting to mobilise in order to move militarily against Slovenia initially, that was something that the SDS leadership favoured co-operating with, that is, the mobilisation effort; whereas their Croatian and Muslim partners in the Government of BH did not want to assist in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D274.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're still in July, it's a telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Dr. Dragan Djokanovic who was the president of the democratic party of federalists, a different party but a pro-Yugoslav one. On page 1 in English and Serbian, line 4, Radovan Karadzic says: "Because Alija has nowhere to go now. It's a dead end. All the legal side is in our hands. And now if they mess up somewhere, Muslims will turn with a vengeance against Alija's intention to go to war." We can see -- we can all see that I'm criticising here people on our side who are doing stupid things and giving Alija a trump card. And now I'm speaking about the Muslim masses. "Those who don't want to go to war, they have a republic. They have no reason to leave Yugoslavia. Alija wants to change that. He wants to go to war and now he cannot explain to the Muslim people why should go to war, but if these people do something stupid, then he can say: Here is the reason why we should go to war."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Now he only needs an alibi for war. We should not help him find one." Do you agree that this is permanent contribution, permanent advocacy, against the war on my part?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if -- permanent advocacy, I wouldn't say that. It's certainly advocating a position at this particular time when there was a war going on in Croatia and there was growing tension in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D276 is the next document I would like to ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from August, 276. August telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik. Page 2 in both Serbian and English. If you remember, at that time we were talking to Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Mr. Filipovic about a historic Serb-Muslim agreement and Krajisnik says: "I was thinking last night. Zulfikarpasic was so convincing, actually he's getting the maximum for his people." And a bit further down Karadzic says: "I think that our hawks can be sorry that they went too. There are some of our people too who say, 'Well, let them start,'" then a profanity, "'so that we can finish it once and for all.'" And then: "Many of our own people will be disappointed if we reach an agreement with the Muslims." And a bit further down, Karadzic says: "Izetbegovic does not care about territory. He cares about quality. If it's 300 square metres, let it be 300 square metres. All he wants is an Islamic state, whereas Zulfikarpasic wants a normal republic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then we need page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see it all. I'm saying that it's a huge turnabout that the Muslim people should declare their preference for Alija or for Adil, Adil meaning Zulfikarpasic. I don't need to read it all. We can all see it for ourselves. And then page 4, Karadzic says: "We don't want to fight you anymore. If you go, we will vote against but we will not fight." Did you review and did you take into account our position taken here against the war and in favour of a historic Muslim-Serb agreement aimed at avoiding the war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the historic -- so-called historic agreement is discussed in the -- certainly in the leadership study. The -- and actions by the hawks that Dr. Karadzic is referring to I believe refers to efforts such as the one in Bosnian Krajina to unite with Croatian Krajina and that would have upset the -- those negotiations in his view. So he opposed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice in Zulfikarpasic's and Filipovic's work that Mr. Izetbegovic supported this initiative and the negotiations throughout July up to August of that year and then he withdrew his support from this historic agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, one of the instances of Izetbegovic suddenly changing his opinion, his stand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D279 is the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my conversation with a friend, a private person, Gojko Djogo from Belgrade but originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 12th of October, 1991, concerning this key session of the Assembly when the declaration of independence was made without the Serbian MPs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 in both languages. Line 6 or 7 from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In the Assembly, Alija Izetbegovic took the floor two or three times and then I had to respond." Djogo says: "Brilliant. They say you told them, 'Gentlemen, we are not going to and you do what you please.'" Karadzic says: "We are letting them, however they are preparing for war. They will try to wage a war here. "Probably as soon as next week." That means that we are expecting even in mid-October that they will start a war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he asks: "Where are they supposed to go to war?" And I'm saying: "They're completely nuts." What I'm asking you is: Were you aware of the level of their military organisation, the level of equipment and weapons they had already in the summer of that year; and if you had known that, would that have made a difference to your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have already dealt with that issue, and I responded "no" to a similar question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 30401 -- 65 ter 30406.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Vojo Kupresanin on the 5th of November, just before our plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kupresanin says: "They are copying, every municipality is making copies and they are all interested, everyone's interested. All the ordinary people are very interested ... even the Muslims are very interested."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I wonder what it's all about," says he. And I say: "Well, they want to vote. The people see that Croatia is falling to pieces." And he says: "Quite unexpected. I personally had about 20 phone calls today from Muslims." And Karadzic says: "Yes, yes, the people want to continue living with us." Is it clear, Dr. Treanor, that we are looking forward to continuing to live together with the Muslims in a common Bosnia and a common Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said any number of times that that was the goal of -- the original goal certainly of the SDS, to keep the whole of Bosnia within Yugoslavia. I believe the exact results of the Serbian plebiscite are cited in the report, indicating how many -- among other things, how many non-Serbs did vote in that plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be MFI'd because of our well-known position on intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1283, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D301 for a moment. D301.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation of the 22nd January 1992, before the joint Assembly session in Bosnia and Herzegovina between Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need Serbian page 11 and English page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Karadzic speaking: "On Friday or Thursday we have a meeting of the Deputies Club. We have to prepare very well. Perhaps our delegation will go to the joint Assembly session ..." And then further down he says: "If the Muslims wanted, we can deal with everything peacefully to everyone's satisfaction, but if not, chaos will begin."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the next page in English. We need page 21 in English, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "If the Muslims are willing, we can deal with everything peacefully so that everyone is satisfied, and if they don't, there will be chaos."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "So that everything is up to them now. I believe they would not be displeased. In fact, I think they could be very happy ..." And then the conversation goes on to deal with something in Turkey, there was some talks going on in Turkey. And it says: "We have to move with the speed of lightning. All these talks were in the framework of a conference." Do you agree that these talks with Mr. Vance and Mr. Carrington were taking place even before February, and here in January it says we have to continue the conference on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, talks involving Mr. Vance and Mr. -- or Lord Carrington were taking place in the fall of 1991. The Carrington negotiations, so-called Hague Conference, evolved into the Cutileiro negotiations, which began in February 1992 involving only Bosnia and the -- Mr. Vance's work in the fall of 1991 resulted in the Vance Plan for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see Karadzic says here: [In English] "We achieved important results which will suit the Muslims too." [Interpretation] Did you bear in mind, did you take into account, that on the 22nd of January, 1992, in my view we had made much progress towards peace and dealing with the situation through peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this conversation is specifically mentioned. The report, of course, especially the leadership study, deals with that negotiating process, which was geared toward a peaceful solution of the crisis, if I can use that word, in BH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P12, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to take a break, Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can. If we could only get more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 25 minutes and resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see P12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree this is from the extended session of the Main and the Executive Boards of the SDS held on the 14th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see English page 5, Serbian 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "Every individual -- it is up to every individual now to do their part of the work and that's what we'll discuss today, but I have to say that we have to be wise, united, and committed," it's towards the bottom of the English page, "to take the last drop of power into our hands in a humane way, of course, carry it all out in a humane way, a fair way, towards both Muslims and Croats who live there, that is particularly important, that there should be no fleeing en masse from our areas." Have you seen this part of my speech at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you put it in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is referenced in the original report. I can't recall whether that specific passage was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a day before this, the first agreement was reached that there would be three Bosnias, on the 13th of February?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Cutileiro negotiations began on the 13th. I think the Lisbon Agreement that you may be referring to was maybe on the 23rd or a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you recall that on 13th of February negotiations began on the transformation of Bosnia and this meeting was held a day later and the talk here is about what had been done and what we would get through this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think I said that the negotiations began the day before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see English page 6. The Serbian part is towards the bottom. I'm saying: "Of course they're trying to hold this referendum under the old, obsolete law ..." The middle of the English page. "Of course they're trying to hold this referendum under the old, obsolete law, that is not in keeping with the current constitution." Next page in Serbian. "That was related to the questions of utility companies, waterworks, and all the other things, where 51 per cent of votes is enough. It is written there that some opinion is either obtained or some statutory instrument is enacted, and if it is passed it is binding. However, in such big issues that are related to the constitution, a two-third majority would be required and that is what we suggested to the German ambassador who visited us, we showed him that conclusion and the papers."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this position I took, that a two-third majority is required, is in keeping with the Cutileiro point number 4?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't recall point 4 in either of the agreements that we have been discussing in connection with those negotiations, that is, the Sarajevo Agreement or the Lisbon Agreement, which came first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not clear enough. The Badinter opinion number 4, the one we displayed yesterday, where it says there has to be a two-third majority.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't recall that -- that opinion said there had to be a two-third majority. Maybe it did. That's easy enough to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 11 in Serbian and 15 in English. 15 in English, 11 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here you see I'm pointing out what would happen if the Serb people were to be tricked over all -- they are taking over everything in the most brutal way without any -- the Serbian people would lose hope. "Firstly, the biggest cowards would leave, and those who are intellectuals, professionals, and others, they would take a briefcase and go abroad. Then those who are less sensitive but have a bit more patriotic feeling would take a briefcase and dash off into Serbia. So in ten years' time or so we would come down to 500 or 600.000 of the poor, who would have no place to go and absolutely no chance to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina. We must not let that happen. If there will be any kind of moving it will be only from their canton to our canton, where we shall ensure the sovereign government of the Serbian people. The map is quite fair. It leaves out all of their villages wherever that is possible. Alija Izetbegovic would say, 'Damn you. While drawing those maps, take care that as few of you as possible stay with us and as few of us possible stay with you?'" So did you take note of that part of the speech and did you take it into account when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've read the speech and it's referenced in my report, so to that extent certainly I took it into account. I don't think I cited this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 65 ter 06640. We can display only the English page because the Serbian is handwritten. So 65 ter 06640 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are notes written by my chef de cabinet at the party headquarters relating to the negotiations with Ambassador Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the Serbian. Page 9 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After Ambassador Cutileiro, Karadzic says: [In English] "We have bad experience with Muslims. They go down on everything we agree upon. The Serbian people are putting us under pressure not to accept a unitary ..." "Essentially they are taking us out of Yugoslavia forever and are closing us into BH. "Freedom first, before money, before bread ..." [Interpretation] Did you know and did you have an insight into this conversation which took place on the 27th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I think the diary is cited in the leadership study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have page 14 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Karadzic says at the top: [In English] "It should be first clarified what certain people want. The people will not accept things which do not correspond to reality and what is not in the interest of the people. "Serbs won't accept independent BH, but they will not attack anyone ..." [Interpretation] Was this known to you and did you take it into account?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the same answer as to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the status of this diary? Has part of this diary been admitted before?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Your Honour, I had the impression it was -- without looking -- it was already in evidence, but it's certainly been referenced before, and I see no reason why it should not be admitted. I don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 65 ter 17555.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are stenographic notes from a meeting of the Deputies Club held on the 28th of February, 1992. And as you know, the 29th of February and the 1st of March was when the referendum was held. These are the stenographic notes or transcript from the meeting of the Deputies Club.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page, please. Actually, it's page 4 in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic: "Yesterday talks were developing in the spirit of what we had seen, a manoeuvre, Mr. Izetbegovic's attempt at a manoeuvre to decrease the significance of what was accomplished in Lisbon. That was certainly a huge pressure on Mr. Cutileiro to decrease the significance of the constituent units."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 6 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is part of my speech. I say: "If they want independence, then we want independence too. "And it's very difficult for them to defend just as it was difficult for the Serbs to defend Yugoslavia because they were accused of wishing to dominate, and so Alija Izetbegovic finds it very difficult to defend his position. And I told Mr. Cutileiro that, we cannot understand why the Muslims do not wish to accept what we have. We have our unit, the Croats have their unit, and the Muslims have their unit, plus our joint organs. "And then Cutileiro said something that most probably Izetbegovic had told him. He said, Yes, but he doesn't have on the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina Turkey, whereas you have Serbia and Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in both versions next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure if we are getting the translation. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, starting with: "Izetbegovic asked for an introduction -- Izetbegovic asked for an introduction, and we agreed, of the national and other criteria. In addition to national criteria, other criteria, as we agreed to it. They said national, geographic, economic, and other criteria. "That suited us too." Now, do you agree, Dr. Treanor, that we accepted everything that could be accepted, that merited acceptance, and we accepted that they were not to be constituent units only on a national basis, but on the economic basis and other criteria as well, traffic and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS position going into these negotiations was that Bosnia should be a confederation with units drawn on an ethnic basis. There was discussion of that, and as a result of that, as indicated here, other -- other criteria were included. But the national criteria remained first, and that is what I believe Mr. Izetbegovic was backing off of after -- a couple of days after the Lisbon Agreement because the -- that had been, as I say, made the first condition -- the first criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 8 in both versions displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says down there: "We spoke of the need to" -- on the left-hand side, "to the necessity of working out the overall Croat and Serb relations and everybody can read what my attitude toward Croatia was. It wasn't our aim that Croatia should not exist, but that it should be rounded off and that it become clear to every Serb that the Serbs and Croats cannot co-exist in a joint state or a joint army" and so on and so forth. Now, the last paragraph: "We looked at the ways and means and principles according to which Serbo-Croatian relations could be resolved regarding Krajina. They think that the best solution would be to relocate the population. That blew the wig off Europeans. They thought that 150- to 250.000 extremely poor Serbs would exchange their rocky country for the richest land properties in Vojvodina. As if the people of Vojvodina would go to that rocky country-side. That's a ridiculous idea." So did you note that we were against any relocation of the population, moving the population anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this passage was cited. I'm not sure what's being discussed here, whether it's Bosnian Krajina or Croatian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're talking about resolving overall Serbo-Croat relations in Yugoslavia. The Croats were advocating relocation, that the Serbs from the poor and rocky areas of Krajina would go to Vojvodina and the Croats of Vojvodina go elsewhere. I say that that is ridiculous. Why would the people of Vojvodina, which is a rich area, go to a rocky, barren area? So this is pre-eminently a stand against the manipulation of the population, and this is something that you should have noted and underlined and taken on board.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not cite this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have P1634 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is -- these are the stenographic notes of the 14th Session of the Assembly of the Serb people of the 27th of March, 1992, so we're getting nearer to the critical days of April now. This is Radovan Karadzic's speech at the Assembly session, and this is his state of mind just three or four days before the war broke out and one day after the massacre in Sijekovac and one day or two days after Izetbegovic's rescinding of the Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 11 of the English and 17 of the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the page there in Serbian - and I'm sure you will be able to find it in English - "We stand straight and pure before God!" That passage. "We stand straight and pure before God! We wanted no divisions. We did not want the destruction of the things that we had in common. Over 73 years we lived in a joint state, denying our plans, disregarding our development, belittling our size and strength, with a view to preserving our joint state. Even in these times we were the last to found a political party to represent our people. We kept on hoping that the forces of unity would prevail over the forces of destruction." Did you include this paragraph and this position and stand, the recapitulation just prior to the beginning of the war into your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I cited this passage, which seems to be a recapitulation of the position that we've discussed any number of times; that is, that the SDS initially certainly wanted the whole of Bosnia to remain within Yugoslavia so that all Serbs would remain within one state. This does not appear to refer to the situation as it existed at this time, in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but just to ensure we don't have unnecessary duplication. If the Registrar could check to see whether the document just admitted as D1285 was not previously admitted as P938, that is, the 28 February 1992 Deputies Club session. Thank you. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be looked into. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "In the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina we fought to preserve a unified Yugoslavia and a united Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our partners did not, however, want Yugoslavia, nor did they want a Bosnia and Herzegovina which would also be ours. They wanted to be the masters of the house and they placed their proprietary name on the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "... but we are pure and clean before God. We have not made a single move which was not provoked."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12 next in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... a pretext which forced us to do that. Perhaps our adversaries, who were supposed to be our partners, led us infallibly exactly where we were supposed to go. Perhaps this is the best and most just because if it passes without bloodshed, maybe all three peoples will flourish. I personally think they will because it is obvious that we cannot live together without hindering one another's development." This, then, is a reference to the transformation of Bosnia into three constituent republics; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the passage seems to refer to the situation which came to a head on October the 15th, that is, the passage of the sovereignty resolutions in the SRBH Assembly by the SDS's coalition partners as the SDA and the HDZ, which would have put the SDS in a -- did put the -- the SDS was the minority and if there had been an independent state, they would have been the minority party in that state. I note the reference to a pretext for action, which seems to get back to the idea of planning in advance that we discussed earlier in my testimony. I would also note the inability of the peoples to live together as an idea being expressed here which is or was the basis of the negotiations at that time. So that -- that is a reference to the ongoing negotiations to divide Bosnia ethnically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, I say here that I believe that all three peoples will flourish once each of them is master in his own house; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I go on to say that: "It is not specific to the Balkans. In the middle of Europe there are communities which cannot live together and they can't because each hampers the development of the other. "And there are many plants in the world that can't grow alongside each other. They have to be separated to flourish. In the highly cultured Europe, Belgium, they are working on this. Switzerland began as a confederation. The smallest canton of 30.000 can now separate, break-away, even form another canton and establish a state of its own ..." and so on and so forth. So is this something you knew about, is this common knowledge to you, that Bosnia could remain but that there should be no domination of one nation over another? Was that the Serb position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the idea of the negotiations was that Bosnia would be divided into ethnic units, each of which would be as independent as possible and would not -- and so that one people would not be able to dominate another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the next paragraph I say: "I must say that our partners' flirtation with Turkey and not only with Turkey but also with extremist fundamentalist regimes in certain Islamic countries have astonished us. It has served to open our eyes." Now, were you aware of our fears and anxiety, and do you know that of late Turkey is making even greater claims on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated -- I think I indicated that I have read this speech and indeed all Dr. Karadzic's speeches in the Assemblies. As to Turkey's claims on Bosnia, I have no idea. I'm not sure what time-period is being referred to, but irrespective of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 23 in English and 37 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic speaking, 23 in English. "Gentlemen, you know that our partners wasted our time for over a year and a half during talks which were always calculated to gain time, without reaching agreement of any sort. We were aware of this, of course, and we worked as if there were no agreement, although we were prepared to abide by any agreements that might be reached. "At a press conference the day before yesterday, Ajanovic definitely stated that it was a trick to gain independence," next page in Serbian, please, "and have Europe recognise them." "They were recognised by Iraq, Turkey, Bulgaria, Libya, and what has changed? However, they have gone so far, with regard to the lunacy of some people, their religious fanaticism and the frenzied state into which they have brought their people, with their promises about a large Bosnian state in which they would be the masters and do whatever they please, that their extremists are prepared to do all sorts of things ..." And then further down: "We have certain indications that -- well, we can count on the fact that they can prepare for war and they might try -- they are attempting something ..." Is that what you say, that we foresaw what would happen? And do you consider that it's a basic prerequisite of intelligence, to anticipate a trick and to be able to avoid it, avoid being duped?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I said that the planning was based on waiting for the other side to make some sort of mistake to -- before making the next move by the Bosnian Serbs. And I think it would be very -- it's a very good thing to be able to anticipate tricks and be able to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 24 in English and 39 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "In Gorazde there is a crazy militant fundamentalist, Hadzo Efendic, who refused any talk. He didn't want to see the Serbs or talk to them. He played some -- he pulled a stunt at a drill" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter needs a reference. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are reading too fast and you need to give reference to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third paragraph in Serbian. "A war in Bosnia and Herzegovina will not solve anything," second paragraph from the top, and this was about Gorazde. And then below: "The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina will not solve anything." Can the participants now see this passage? "If it begins, you will get plans." But further below it says: "Let the situation be studied to protect and defend lives, territory, and property. We have no other plans."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, do you agree that up to this 27th of March, throughout those months I always advocated peace and peaceful solutions, never, ever advocating war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think there was an attempt to reach a peaceful settlement. The SDS and Dr. Karadzic had certain goals which are talked about extensively here, that is, remaining in Yugoslavia or changing BH into a confederation. If those could be achieved peacefully, so much the better. I think everyone would prefer to achieve their goals peacefully rather than through war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this is the 27th of March, four or five days before the war, and still we have no plans for war, and I'm saying that openly at this meeting. Explicitly I say here: "We have no other plans."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says. I'm not sure what -- what that may mean in regard to particular plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at your report and see how it treated the aspect of regionalisation. Let's look at paragraph -- that is, page 5, item E in your introduction. 65 ter 592. E5. [In English] "Throughout 1992 the Bosnian Serb leadership pursued a policy of 'regionalisation,' which meant organising areas in which Serbs represented the relative majority into district regions through the concept of 'communities of municipalities.' By initiating the creation of the regional bodies of authority throughout BH, the SDS thus began preparation quite early for eventual de facto take-over of the Serb-populated territories in BH. Many of the preparations were conducted conspiratorially and in secret." [Interpretation] In all these territories, there was a majority Serb population; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "all these territories." If you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not been interpreted correctly. It says here -- you say that Serbs on the territories where they were a majority, does that mean that Serb-populated territories are territories where Serbs are a majority and where at the elections they were victorious? [In English] "... eventual de facto take-over of Serb-populated territories in BH ..."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reference to the Serb-majority areas in connection with communities of municipalities is primarily a reference to the municipalities in which the Serbs formed either an absolute or a relative majority strong enough to have enabled them at the municipal elections in November 1990 to come to power in those municipalities. Those were the municipalities which joined the new communities of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So take-over and take power. In our language there is a distinction between taking power and taking over. Do you agree that in those municipalities the Serbs and the SDS had power; they did not need to take it over from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two issues there as far as taking power.
